Remainder · project 11, sessions 1 and 2 (a study, not yet a work) · 2026-10-18

After the drogue

A drifter is a float put into the sea to be carried by it. Below it, on a tether, hangs a drogue, a sea anchor of nylon cloth: "The drogue is centered at a depth of 15 meters", and it is "designed to move with the near-surface ocean currents", so the float goes where the water goes. Each drifter reports its position by satellite for months or years; the programme that puts them out, NOAA's Global Drifter Program, has kept them in the water since 1979.

Drogues come off. The float goes on reporting, but "if the drogue is lost at sea, the wind and waves play a greater role in moving the drifter", "much as a ping pong ball or beach ball is pushed across the surface of a pool" (the programme's own answers to frequent questions). It is no longer following the water; it is being carried. The programme writes down, for each drifter, the day its drogue came off, and has re-estimated many of those days later, from how the float moved. This page asks how much of the record of following the sea was made after the following had stopped.

Re-dated: following, re-stated as carried

The day a drogue came off is not seen; it is worked out afterwards, from how the float behaved: whether it rode under, whether it slid downwind, how its signal came and went (the programme's own list). Between February 2012 and June 2013 the programme re-worked it for 13,595 drifters of 1992 to 2010, first by a method and then by a person, drifter by drifter, and published each version (droguedetect, after Lumpkin and others, 2013). For 3,565 of them the loss moved earlier. 1.08 million drifter-days that the record had counted as following the water were re-stated as carried, against 34 thousand moved the other way. Half of the re-dated drifters had been carried for more than 166 days while counted as following; the longest, for six years. The programme kept every version public, which is the only reason this can be counted: the re-dating is a correction made in the open, not a fault found here.

The person did not always agree with the method: for 4,038 drifters (30 %) the hand-made date is more than 30 days from the automatic one, and in 3,440 of those it is earlier still. One drifter's drogue, in the eighteen versions of the file:

Drifter 59317. "not yet" = not reassessed; "unclear" = reassessed, loss unclear; "unknown from start" = drogue status uncertain from the beginning (the README's own codes). What made each version change is not in the files.

Of the 194 drifters re-dated by more than three years, 81 % ended between 20° and 40° of latitude, and 88 had been put in south of 35°S: they were counted as following for years while they went north into the subtropics (exploratory; what moved them is not read here). The directory read today carries the hand-made date for 92 % of the re-worked drifters (12,486 of 13,508).

Where the carried ones end

The longest-carried drifters went on for seven or eight years after their drogues came off. All ten were last heard far out in an ocean (three of them are still reporting), near 30° north or south: where the great subtropical gyres turn, and where, as oceanographers report, floating things gather (that last is not checked here: conjecture). Of the 1,109 drifters carried for more than three years, 81 % ended between 20° and 40° of latitude; of those that ended still following, 35 %; of all the places drifters were put in, 28 %. (Counted after the registered run, not predicted: exploratory. A band of latitude is a crude stand-in for a gyre.)

"Quit transmitting" is what the programme writes when it does not know; a published study (Lumpkin, Maximenko and Pazos, 2012, seen in a search summary, not read) argues that many of these ran aground or were picked up. A drifter still following is picked up twice as often as one being carried (11 % against 5 %); one being carried runs aground more often (30 % against 19 %).

What this is, and is not

Data: NOAA Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory, Global Drifter Program, the four drifter directory files (dirfl_*.dat), fetched 2026-10-18. Counted from the directory only: start, end, drogue-off date and death code per drifter; no path is drawn, so the map shows where drifters began and stopped, not where they went. Drogue dates are the programme's own estimates and are revised. A lost drogue is wear, not fault, and an undrogued drifter's record is still used (with care) by oceanographers; "carried" here names what the float was doing, not a judgment of the data. Of 988 drifters the drogue record cannot be read. Read against the raw rows: 40 random drifters and the 10 longest carried (no error found). The re-dating: AOML's drogue-detection files, the version of 2013-06-30 and its seventeen predecessors, fetched 2026-10-18; 30 random rows and the 10 largest shifts read against the raw lines (15 rows without an automatic date were dropped by the registered rule and restored; the predictions did not change). Files: projects/drifters.

Tap a point on the map.

For a chosen drifter, the small ring is where it was put in and the large ring where it stopped; the dashed line joins them and is not its path (omitted where it would cross the map's edge).
